Issued at 128 PM CST Tue Nov 24 2026

Surface high pressure was centered just northwest of the cwa at
midday, with a few surface obs reporting near 1038 mb in the 
IA/MN/WI border region. Northeast low-level flow around the high
had pushed a weak band of lake-effect rain/snow showers across 
northwest IN and parts of northeast IL earlier this morning, 
though this activity has weakened as mid-level subsidence 
continues to lower inversion heights. That said, can't rule out 
a stray sprinkle (an maybe a wet flake or two) along the IL lake
shore this afternoon as what's left of the band affects 
northern Cook/Lake (IL) counties. Otherwise, quiet weather 
conditions are expected through Wednesday morning, with only a 
gradually thickening layer of high clouds developing across the 
region. 

Attention then shifts to the complex storm system forecast to 
develop across the central and eastern CONUS during the mid-late
week period, including the Thanksgiving holiday. Latest 12Z 
guidance continues to be in good agreement that the primary 
focus for accumulating snow with this system continues to be 
portions of western and central IL, with rain the primary 
precipitation type across our forecast area from late Wednesday 
through Friday. Some slushy accums do appear possible across our
southwest tier of counties mainly Wednesday night, though at 
this time guidance continues to depict more significant amounts 
across portions of the WFO LSX/ILX forecast areas southwest of 
our cwa.

GOES vapor imagery and 12Z upper air analysis depict a large 
scale upper trough axis from the Canadian prairies southward 
across the Plains into Texas. Several smaller-scale short wave 
disturbances are noted within this trough, most notably (for our
local concerns) a potent vort digging into the trough from 
southern Saskatchewan. Another strong wave was transiting the 
base of the long-wave trough across TX. The potent northern wave
is progged to dig southeast across the mid/lower Missouri 
Valley region into Wednesday, resulting in the development of a 
closed mid/upper level low across IA/MO in the process. At the 
surface, this manifests late Wednesday into Thursday as an 
inverted trough developing from IA into the lower MO/OH valleys 
in the wake of our retreating surface high over the Great Lakes.
As the mid/upper level low deepens, this results in increasing 
warm/moist advection into our region from the southeast and 
east, which is somewhat atypical for autumn/winter storms in the
Midwest. Thus the coldest air aloft is forecast to remain 
within the vicinity of the mid/upper level circulation, where 
dynamic cooling is strongest, while thermal profiles to the east
(across much of our forecast area) warm and moisten within the 
east-southeast flow east of the mid-level circulation center.

Precipitation is forecast to develop from south to north 
Wednesday afternoon/evening as the system develops to our west, 
though it will be fighting lingering low-level dry air 
associated with the retreating surface high. Latest guidance 
focuses highest pops across our southern/western cwa through 
Wednesday night in this scenario. Forecast soundings indicate 
some potential for a snow/rain mix especially at onset, mainly 
southwest of a Rockford-Rantoul IL line. This area of rain/snow 
then looks to pivot across our southwest/south counties late 
Wednesday night before low-level profiles and wet-bulbs warm 
into Thursday morning. Overall, NBM thermal fields and surface 
dew points appear a little too warm Wednesday/Wednesday night, 
though even nudging those lower with blended raw model guidance 
keeps any slushy snow accumulation limited to a few tenths of an
inch or less in our far southwest near ILX's border. NBM pops 
also are lagging the latest model trends of being lower/drier 
with northeastward extent through Thursday morning, so did nudge
these down across our far north/northeast as well, especially 
Wednesday afternoon/night. The mid-level low is then forecast to
drift slowly east across the lower OH/Tennessee valleys 
Thursday and Thursday night, with precipitation in the easterly 
warm-conveyor north of the circulation changing to all rain. 
The area of precipitation then likely pivots across our south 
and southeastern cwa by Thursday night and gradually pulls away
to the east on Friday. With PWAT values in the 0.90" range 
within the moist conveyor (~200 percent of normal for late 
November), QPF amounts depict total rainfall amounts from 1 to 
nearly 1.5 inches south of I-80 by the time precip ends Friday. 

While guidance is in good agreement in bringing another lower 
amplitude and more progressive short wave across the area Friday
night into early Saturday, this wave looks to be moisture-
starved. Ensembles suggest an active pattern will persist into 
early next week however, with some additional precipitation 
chances as early as Sunday. Though more active, near to slightly
